Notifications for Python, imported as `egradx.notification`. It is the counterpart of the Java `egradx-notification` and the Node `@babulvaibhav/egradx-notification`, with the same tables, rules, endpoints and wire format. The three SDKs can share one database and one outbox:
- any SDK delivers what another queued, and never twice;
- any SDK reads the others' inboxes, delivery log and bulk sends;
- any SDK decrypts the channel secrets another stored.

## What it does

| Export | What it is |
|---|---|
| `EgradxNotifications(engine, NotificationsOptions(...))` | Everything below, on the application's SQLAlchemy `AsyncEngine`. Call `start()` from the application's startup (FastAPI's lifespan) to start the dispatcher, and `await close()` at shutdown. |
| `messenger.send(EgradxMessageRequest.on(channel)…build())` | Sends to users (through `recipient_resolver`) or to addresses, from a template or from ready-made content. Every check happens before anything is queued, and each recipient's language gets its own message. A bulk send is `to_organization_members()` or `to_all_users()`; it is capped, then expanded in the background. |
| `transport.submit(message)` | The level beneath the messenger: rendered content to addresses that are already resolved. |
| `dispatcher` | Delivers the outbox. It claims deliveries with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and a lease, sends concurrently, retries with backoff, and marks a delivery `DEAD` when retrying can't help. It also runs the retention cleanup. |
| `deliveries` | The delivery log (filter by status, channel, or the request that sent it), bulk-send progress, and `requeue`. |
| `templates`, `template_service` | Handlebars templates, looked for in this order: the organization's stored template, the one stored for all organizations, the application's template directories, then the library's own. The type's variables are enforced strictly. Rendering is this SDK's own Handlebars (`handlebars.py`, no third-party engine), held to `contracts/notification-templates/rendering-test-vectors.json` as Java's and Node's renderers are. |
| `channel_configs` | Per-organization channel settings. Secrets are encrypted, and are never returned. |
| Channels | `email` (SMTP, through aiosmtplib), `slack`, `webhook` (HMAC-signed), `sms` (Twilio), `whatsapp` (Meta, Twilio), and `log` (for development). You can add your own: any object with `channel` and `async send(request)`, optionally `unavailable_for`, `validate_address`, `validate_content` and `validate_configuration`. |
| `publish_to_user`, `publish_to_organization`, `publish_to_platform`, `inbox`, `connections` | In-app notifications, the inbox, and the live stream. Inside an `egradx_transaction`, a notification is pushed to live streams only after the commit. |
| `egradx.notification.fastapi.notification_routes(notifications)` | Every path in `contracts/openapi/notification.yaml`: the inbox and its stream, `/admin/**` for one organization, and `/admin/platform/**` beyond it. Install with the `fastapi` extra. |
| `await migrate_notification(database_url)` | Applies `contracts/db/postgresql/notification` into `egradx_notification_schema_history`, the history table Java uses. The wheel carries the SQL and the library's templates. |

## Sending

```python
await notifications.messenger.send(EgradxMessageRequest.on("email")
    .organization(org_id)
    .template("order.shipped", {"customerName": name, "orderNumber": number})
    .to_users(customer_id)
    .attach(attachment("invoice.pdf", "application/pdf", pdf))
    .build())
```

Inside `async with egradx_transaction(engine):`, the message is queued if and only if the business change commits, and the dispatcher is woken after the commit. `messenger.send` never publishes an in-app notification: to do both, make both calls.

## What the application supplies

| Option | Why | Without it |
|---|---|---|
| `types` | The kinds of message it sends, with their variables (`EgradxNotificationType.builder(key)…build()`). | Only the library's own channel-test type exists. |
| `template_directories` | Its template files, laid out as `<key>/<channel>[.<locale>].(subject\|body).(txt\|html)`. Every file is checked at startup. | Only stored templates and the library's own. |
| `recipient_resolver`, `recipient_directory`, `recipient_preferences` | Who a user is on a channel, who belongs to an audience, and who opted out. In Java, `egradx-notification-auth` provides these from egradx-auth; in Python, they arrive with step 6d. | User ids can't be resolved. Bulk sends are refused. Nobody has opted out. |
| `viewers`, `actors` | Who is calling the inbox and admin endpoints, and the `egradx.notification.*` authorities they hold. | Those endpoints answer 401. |
| `secrets_passphrase`, or `EGRADX_NOTIFICATION_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE` (else `EGRADX_SECURITY_CRYPTO_PASSPHRASE`) | Encrypts channel secrets. Use the same passphrase as the Java and Node applications on the same database. | Saving a secret is refused. |
| `built_in_channels=BuiltInChannels(email=ApplicationEmail(SmtpTransport(...), sender=...))` | The application's own mail server, for organizations without stored settings. | Email needs stored settings. |
| `broadcaster` | Gets a published notification to the live streams of every instance (for example through Redis pub/sub, calling `deliver_locally` on each). | Live pushes reach this instance's streams only. |

The defaults are Java's: 500 recipients per message, a 5-minute lease, a 2-minute send timeout, 8 attempts with backoff from 30 seconds, a cap of 1000 on bulk audiences, and retention of 30 days for sent deliveries, 90 days for dead ones, and 365 days for in-app notifications. Durations are in seconds (`DispatcherSettings(lease_seconds=300)`).

## Metrics and traces

Sending, submitting, bulk sends and every delivery attempt are observed, and dead, discarded, enqueued and published messages counted, as Java does ([the guide](/docs/guides/observability)). There are gauges for the backlog and open streams. Each message stores the trace, the request id and the trace context of the request that submitted it, so a delivery's span is a child of that request's and its log lines carry its request id. Set `observations` and `metrics` in `NotificationsOptions`; by default they use the global OpenTelemetry providers. `backlog_refresh_seconds` is Java's `egradx.notification.metrics.backlog-refresh`.

## Not ported

- `egradx-notification-auth`. It arrives with Python auth (step 6d).

## Tests

The tests run against a real PostgreSQL (`EGRADX_TEST_PG_*`):
- The renderer is held to the contract's rendering test vectors.
- The HTTP channels are tested against a local stand-in server, and email against a local SMTP server (aiosmtpd, a development dependency only).
- Every endpoint is validated against the OpenAPI contract.
- Where the Java test databases exist, Python reads Java's inboxes, outbox and bulk sends, and sends with a secret Java stored.

Import from `egradx.notification`.

### `EgradxNotificationBacklogGauge`

```python
class EgradxNotificationBacklogGauge
```

egradx.notification.delivery.backlog: PENDING deliveries that are due now (`egradx.state` = `due`) and those
waiting for a retry (`waiting`). A `due` count that keeps growing means sends are falling behind, or no dispatcher
is running. Counted in one pass over the PENDING rows, and kept for `refresh_seconds`, so that several instances each
scraped often do not each count the table. As Java's EgradxNotificationBacklogGauge, with one difference: a gauge is
read synchronously, often on the metric reader's thread, so a stale count starts a recount on the event loop and the
last count is reported meanwhile (NaN before the first).

#### Constructor

```python
def __init__(engine: AsyncEngine, now: Callable[[], datetime], refresh_seconds: float, metrics: EgradxMetrics) -> None
```

### `EgradxBackoffPolicy`

```python
class EgradxBackoffPolicy
```

Exponential backoff with jitter: retry n waits initial × multiplier^(n-1), capped, then spread by ±jitter so a
batch that failed together does not retry together. The defaults ride out about an hour of provider outage. As
Java's EgradxBackoffPolicy.

#### Constructor

```python
def __init__(initial_seconds: float = 30, multiplier: float = 2, max_seconds: float = 3600, jitter: float = 0.2, random_source: Callable[[], float] = random.random) -> None
```

### `EgradxBulkExpander`

```python
class EgradxBulkExpander
```

Turns bulk sends into deliveries, one page of recipients per call, each page one transaction: lock the oldest
send still expanding (skipping any another instance holds), take the next page after expanded_through, resolve,
render once per language, write the deliveries, move on. A page that fails rolls back and is done again; nobody is
expanded twice or skipped. Users without an address, or who opted out, are counted, not failed. A template that no
longer renders fails the send; anything else is retried on the next poll. As Java's EgradxBulkExpander.

#### Constructor

```python
def __init__(engine: AsyncEngine, directory: EgradxRecipientDirectory | None, resolver: EgradxRecipientResolver | None, preferences: EgradxRecipientPreferences | None, templates: EgradxTemplateEngine, page_size: int, now: Callable[[], datetime], logger: logging.Logger, observations: EgradxObservations | None = None, metrics: EgradxMetrics | None = None) -> None
```

#### `expand_once`

```python
async def expand_once() -> bool
```

Returns whether a page was expanded, so the caller comes straight back for another.

### `EgradxNotificationDispatcher`

```python
class EgradxNotificationDispatcher
```

Delivers what the outbox holds. Each round claims a batch of due deliveries in one statement, sends them
concurrently outside any transaction, then records each result on its own; nothing holds a connection or a lock
while a provider is answering.

Safe to run on every instance, and alongside the Java and Node dispatchers on the same database: claiming uses
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and counts the attempt up front, hiding the row for the lease; every result is written only
if the row still has that attempt and is PENDING, so a slow sender's result whose lease lapsed is discarded rather
than overwriting a newer attempt. Delivery is at-least-once. As Java's EgradxNotificationDispatcher.

#### Constructor

```python
def __init__(engine: AsyncEngine, channels: EgradxChannelRegistry, attachments: EgradxAttachmentStore, settings: DispatcherSettings, backoff: EgradxBackoffPolicy, retention: RetentionSettings, bulk: EgradxBulkExpander | None, now: Callable[[], datetime], logger: logging.Logger, observations: EgradxObservations | None = None, metrics: EgradxMetrics | None = None) -> None
```

#### `cleanup`

```python
async def cleanup() -> int
```

Deletes SENT and DEAD deliveries past their retention, messages left with no deliveries, in-app notifications
past theirs, and finished bulk sends with nothing left. Public so an operator can run it. Returns how many
deliveries were deleted.

opposite responses, and only a channel can tell them apart; one that can't should answer retryable. A channel
that raises is treated as retryable.


Delivered: recorded SENT with the provider's id for it, if it gives one.

#### `retryable`

```python

```

Not delivered, but might be later: rescheduled with backoff, until attempts run out.

#### `permanent`

```python

```

Not delivered, and trying again will not help: recorded DEAD at once.


available; the library's own email channel is nothing more. As Java's EgradxNotificationChannel: bound every

### `EgradxMessenger`

```python
class EgradxMessenger
```

The way to send a message: to users or addresses, on the channel the caller names, from a template or ready-made
content. Returns once queued; nothing is sent here. Resolves each user to an address and a locale, renders once
per locale, and queues one message per locale, all in one transaction (the surrounding one, if any): every
locale's message is queued or none is. It never publishes an in-app notification; a caller wanting both makes both
calls. As Java's EgradxMessenger.

#### Constructor

```python
def __init__(deps: MessengerDependencies) -> None
```

#### `send`

```python
async def send(request: EgradxMessageRequest, connection: AsyncConnection | None = None) -> EgradxSendReceipt
```

Raises EgradxUnreachableRecipientsException if a user has no address on the channel (unless skipped),
EgradxTemplateException if the template is missing or the model breaks its type's contract,
EgradxChannelUnavailableException if the channel is not configured for the organization, and
ValidationException for a malformed address or a limit exceeded.

### `EgradxOutboxTransport`

```python
class EgradxOutboxTransport
```

The default transport: writes the message and one PENDING delivery per address, for the dispatcher to deliver;
needs no broker. As Java's EgradxOutboxTransport:

- it joins the surrounding egradx_transaction (or `connection`), so an order confirmation goes out if and only
  if the order commits; without one it runs in its own;
- everything knowable before sending is checked here, on the caller's side: the channel exists and is configured
  for the organization, every address is well-formed, the limits hold;
- the trace and request id are stored with the message, so its deliveries can be found by, and traced to, the request
  that sent them (egradx.notification.submit).



### `EgradxFileTemplates`

```python
class EgradxFileTemplates
```

Templates shipped as files, indexed once when created; the counterpart of Java's classpath templates, with the
same layout under each directory:

    order.shipped/email.subject.txt       subject, default locale
    order.shipped/email.body.html         body; .html means values are HTML-escaped
    order.shipped/email.fr.body.html      French
    order.shipped/sms.body.txt            .txt means values are inserted as they are

The application's directories are searched in order, then the library's; the first holding a template for a key,
channel and locale supplies it. Every file is checked now: its name, its type being declared, compiling, and
using only declared variables. A typo fails startup, not a send.

### `EgradxHandlebarsRenderer`

```python
class EgradxHandlebarsRenderer
```

Handlebars, strict and treating templates as untrusted, as Java's EgradxHandlebarsRenderer:

- a top-level variable the template uses but the model lacks fails the render, naming it;
- the model is converted to plain data first (maps, lists, strings, numbers, booleans), so a template reads
  what it is given and nothing else; partials are refused;
- escaping follows the format: HTML-escaped into an HTML body, verbatim into text. Subjects are text, with line
  breaks collapsed to spaces, since a mail subject is one header line.

Compiled templates are cached by the source's cache key, bounded in number.

#### Constructor

```python
def __init__(cache_size: int = 500) -> None
```

```python

```


Compiles without rendering, so a syntax error is refused when a template is saved or loaded.

### `EgradxNotificationType`

```python
class EgradxNotificationType
```

One kind of message an application sends (`order.shipped`) and the variables its templates may use.

The declaration makes rendering strict: a required variable missing from the model is refused, an optional
one may be left out, a model entry that is neither is refused (it is almost always a misspelling), and a
template using an undeclared variable is refused when loaded or saved. As Java's EgradxNotificationType.

| `description` | `str | None` |  |
| `required` | `tuple[str, ...]` |  |
| `optional` | `tuple[str, ...]` |  |
| `replaceable` | `bool` | `False` |
| `user_can_opt_out` | `bool` | `False` |

### `check_template`

```python
def check_template(type_: EgradxNotificationType, source: EgradxTemplateSource, renderer: EgradxTemplateRenderer) -> None
```

Refuses a template that does not compile, or that uses a variable its type does not declare, by rendering it
once with a stand-in for every declared variable. Best effort: a variable used only in a branch the stand-ins
don't take isn't seen here, but rendering is strict, so it still fails at send. The stand-in is an empty map,
as in Java: false in {{#if}}, nothing to iterate, empty nested fields.

present as None, which is what lets the strict renderer tell "optional and absent" from "never declared". As
Java's EgradxTemplateContract.prepareModel.
